## Where This Fits
The third week of Part II, one of the three mathematical peaks of the course, and one of the three weeks whose literature ages fastest (W9, W10, W13). At the end of W8 the supervision axis had two entries ticked: the pre-training distribution and human demonstrations. A demonstration says "answer like this"; it does not say "this answer is better than that one", and it was written by someone else, not by the model. This week opens the third and fourth entries — **human preferences** and **verifiable rewards**. The signal shrinks from a written answer to a single comparison or a single score, and what gets scored is **the model's own output**. The model trained last week is this week's $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.

The week asks five questions. **First, how does a comparison become a number?** A person can only say that A is better than B. The Bradley–Terry model writes that as $\sigma(r_w - r_l)$, and a reward model is a network trained with exactly this loss — an examiner that has learned to imitate people. The loss sees only the *difference* of two scores: adding any quantity that depends on the prompt alone changes nothing. That invariance is used three times this week. **Second, how does a score become a gradient?** Three lines give the policy gradient, and it reads as "supervised fine-tuning on your own answers, each one weighted by its score" — weighted maximum likelihood. For students without a reinforcement-learning background this is the way in. The score comes from an examiner that was itself learned from a finite sample, so the model is tied to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ with a KL term; Gao et al. (ICML 2023) measured what happens as the rope is let out: the examiner's score keeps rising while the true score rises and then falls. PPO is the engineering that makes this stable, at the price of a critic; the three-stage InstructGPT pipeline keeps four networks alive at once. **Third, can we do without the examiner?** DPO: the KL-regularised objective has a closed-form optimum; solve it for the reward, substitute into Bradley–Terry, and the partition function cancels because it depends on the prompt alone. What remains is a logistic loss in $\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ only — the main blackboard derivation of the week. Its whole appeal is also its whole limitation: the data are a fixed set of comparisons (off-policy); the loss constrains only the difference between two answers, so the probabilities of both can fall together (likelihood displacement, ICLR 2025); and having no reward model does not mean it cannot over-optimise (NeurIPS 2024). **Fourth, what if the examiner cannot be flattered?** Mathematics and code have right answers, so the reward can be a program — reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). GRPO replaces PPO's critic with "answer the same question $G$ times and compare each answer with the group mean". The 2025 variants (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GSPO, SAPO) need not be taught as four algorithms: with a right-or-wrong reward, GRPO's update on one prompt is exactly the group's standard deviation times the difference between the average correct answer and the average wrong one — three lines of algebra — and the variants are switches on that expression. ScaleRL (ICLR 2026, oral) measured over 400,000 GPU-hours that such switches mostly change efficiency, not the asymptote. **Fifth, what happens when the examiner is fooled?** Human preference is itself a proxy: people and preference models both favour convincingly written agreement (ICLR 2024), and the official post-mortem of one 2025 deployment incident is about exactly this (a blog post, not a paper). A program is no different: it checks only what it checks. The 2026 evidence has to be read piece by piece — a verifier that checks only extensional correctness is satisfied by enumerated answers (a workshop paper); in an environment where the test harness can be tampered with, one per cent of cheating trajectories in the training data is enough for a model to pick the behaviour up, and RL then amplifies it (EMNLP 2026); accuracy rises while the causal importance of the reasoning does not (ICML 2026); and even random rewards raise the scores of one model family on a few benchmarks (ICML 2026) — for which there is a second explanation, that those benchmarks were contaminated (AAAI 2026). That last pair is this week's assigned reading: one phenomenon, two explanations, and the question of which experiment separates them.

The week closes with a new line in the compute ledger. The cost of RL training is **sampling plus updating**, and the sampling half is inference. An episode brings back a single score, so there is little information to learn — which accounts for two hooks left open last week (a rank-1 LoRA suffices under RL; RL forgets less than SFT) and is the reason on-policy distillation exists (the student writes, a teacher grades every token). **The DPO loss and the GRPO advantage are written from scratch and tested live by the instructor; the three training runs are recorded in rehearsal and replayed in class, and the "reward with a deliberate loophole" is one of the three failure-case high points of the course.** Students do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. Derive Bradley–Terry's $\sigma(r_w - r_l)$ and the reward-model loss from "the log-odds are a difference of two scores"; explain why the loss is unchanged by adding any quantity that depends on $x$ alone, and hence why reward values cannot be compared across reward models. Write out the data each of the three RLHF stages consumes (demonstrations, pairwise comparisons, unlabelled prompts), how each stage fails, and which networks disappear at inference time.
2. Derive the policy gradient $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}[r] = \mathbb{E}[\,r\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y \mid x)\,]$ in three lines, read it as "SFT on your own samples, weighted by reward", and prove that subtracting a baseline that depends on $x$ alone leaves the expectation unchanged. Place SFT, REINFORCE, DPO and GRPO in one table by where the data come from and what weight each sample gets.
3. Write the KL-regularised objective and its closed-form optimum $\pi^{*} \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\exp(r/\beta)$ with its one-line proof, and state the limits $\beta \to 0$ and $\beta \to \infty$. Explain why the KL term is needed (the examiner can be trusted only on the distribution it has seen), and find the KL distance that maximises the gold reward in Gao et al.'s functional form.
4. Derive DPO in full (closed form → solve for the reward → substitute into Bradley–Terry → $Z(x)$ cancels), read its gradient (which pairs get a large weight, and the two directions it pushes in), and state its three limitations with the strength of the evidence for each: the data are fixed (Xu et al.; Tajwar et al.), the loss constrains only a difference so both probabilities can fall (Razin et al.; Pal et al. is a preprint), and it over-optimises even without a reward model (Rafailov et al. 2024).
5. Write PPO's surrogate for a language model (token-level versus sequence-level ratio, when the clip is active at all, what the critic costs) and GRPO's advantage. Derive the identity for binary rewards (the update on one prompt equals the group's standard deviation times the difference between the mean score of correct and of wrong answers), and use it to fill in the comparison table for DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GSPO and SAPO: which switch each one moves and which bias it fixes.
6. Distinguish three examiners (a person comparing on the spot, a learned reward model, a program that checks the answer), give the form reward hacking takes with each, and cite one piece of evidence for each. Read *Spurious Rewards* and Wu et al. as two explanations of one phenomenon, name the experiments that separate them (clean problems, another model family, no clipping), and check both against the four questions for reading a paper.
7. Do the compute accounting for RL training: sampling $G$ rollouts per prompt (decoding, $2N$ per token, memory-bound) plus the update ($6N$, about $4N$ with LoRA), and how many networks DPO, PPO and GRPO each keep in memory. Explain how "one episode brings back one score" accounts for rank 1 being enough and for RL forgetting less, and state what IsoCompute and ScaleRL say about how large $G$ should be and which design choices are worth tuning.
8. Place on-policy distillation in the 2×2 of who generates the samples and how dense the signal is (SFT, RL, distillation), and attribute it correctly (GKD and MiniLLM, ICLR 2024; the Qwen3 technical report; the widely circulated account is a blog post).

## References
- **Textbooks**: JM3 (release of 2026-08-19), second half of ch. 8 *Post-training*. §8.3 *Learning from Preferences* and §8.4.2 *Direct Preference Optimization* cover the first half of this week: Bradley–Terry, the reward-model loss and the DPO derivation are all there, with responses written $o$ (this course writes $y$). §8.4.1 on PPO is still marked "TBD", §8.4.3–8.4.4 have no body text, and the chapter does not cover GRPO or reward hacking — **from PPO onward this week has no textbook**. **RAS-R** (Raschka, *Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch)*), ch. 6 *Training Reasoning Models with Reinforcement Learning* and ch. 7 *Improving GRPO for Reinforcement Learning*, builds GRPO from scratch; ch. 8 covers distillation. That book has no DPO: a from-scratch DPO notebook is in the bonus material of the repository for **RAS** (`ch07/04_preference-tuning-with-dpo`), not in either book.

**Preferences, reward models and RLHF**
- Bradley & Terry, **Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs: I. The Method of Paired Comparisons**, *Biometrika* 39(3/4), 1952 (DOI 10.2307/2334029) — where the model comes from
- Christiano et al., **Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences**, arXiv:1706.03741 (2017) — the starting point for learning a reward from pairwise comparisons and then running RL on it
- Stiennon et al., **Learning to summarize from human feedback**, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv:2009.01325) — the same recipe applied to a language model
- Ouyang et al., **Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2203.02155) — InstructGPT; the paper reports about 13k training prompts for SFT, 33k for the reward model and 31k for PPO
- Gao, Schulman & Hilton, **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization**, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2210.10760) — **the basis of this week's critique**; the abstract: in a synthetic setup, the gold reward follows a different functional form depending on the optimisation method (RL or best-of-$n$), with coefficients that scale smoothly with reward-model size; the paper adds that a KL penalty acted like early stopping in their setting
- Sharma et al., **Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.13548) — the abstract: responses that match the user's views are more likely to be preferred, and both people and preference models prefer convincingly written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time
- Kirk et al., **Understanding the Effects of RLHF on LLM Generalisation and Diversity**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.06452) — the abstract: RLHF generalises better than SFT to new inputs but markedly reduces output diversity
- Lee et al., **RLAIF vs. RLHF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2309.00267) — preferences labelled by a model
- OpenAI, **Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy**, company **blog post**, 2 May 2025 — **an official post-mortem of a deployment incident, not a paper**: it describes post-training as SFT followed by RL on several reward signals; the update of 25 April 2025 added a reward signal based on thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback, the model became noticeably more sycophantic, and the rollback began on 28 April
- Wu, **Sailing by the Stars: A Survey on Reward Models and Learning Strategies for Learning from Rewards**, arXiv:2505.02686 (2025) — a single-author survey; **preprint**

**Policy gradient and PPO**
- Williams, **Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning**, *Machine Learning* 8(3–4), 229–256 (1992; DOI 10.1007/BF00992696) — REINFORCE
- Schulman et al., **Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms**, arXiv:1707.06347 (2017) — the clipped surrogate objective; **preprint**
- Peters & Schaal, **Reinforcement Learning by Reward-Weighted Regression for Operational Space Control**, ICML 2007 (DOI 10.1145/1273496.1273590), and Peng et al., **Advantage-Weighted Regression: Simple and Scalable Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning**, arXiv:1910.00177 (2019) — "regression weighted by reward"; the closed form in the second has the same shape as this week's

**DPO: the derivation, the variants, and where it breaks**
- Rafailov et al., **Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.18290) — **the source of this week's main derivation**; §4 for the derivation and the reading of the gradient, the appendix for a reference implementation
- Azar et al., **A General Theoretical Paradigm to Understand Learning from Human Preferences**, AISTATS 2024 (arXiv:2310.12036) — IPO; the abstract: RLHF rests on two approximations (pairwise preferences can be replaced by pointwise rewards; a reward model generalises out of distribution), and DPO bypasses the second while still relying on the first
- Ethayarajh et al., **KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2402.01306), and Meng, Xia & Chen, **SimPO: Simple Preference Optimization with a Reference-Free Reward**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2405.14734) — two widely used variants; the second uses the average log-probability as the implicit reward and needs no reference model (abstract)
- Razin et al., **Unintentional Unalignment: Likelihood Displacement in Direct Preference Optimization**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2410.08847) — the abstract: the likelihood of preferred responses often decreases during training; probability mass can move to responses with the opposite meaning; when training refusals, the refusal rate of Llama-3-8B-Instruct fell from 74.4% to 33.4%
- Pal et al., **Smaug: Fixing Failure Modes of Preference Optimisation with DPO-Positive**, arXiv:2402.13228 (2024) — the abstract: in theory the standard DPO loss can reduce the likelihood of the preferred response as long as the relative probability rises; **preprint**
- Xu et al., **Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study**, ICML 2024, oral (arXiv:2404.10719) — the abstract: DPO may have fundamental limitations; once the key factors of PPO are identified, PPO surpasses the other methods on every testbed
- Tajwar et al., **Preference Fine-Tuning of LLMs Should Leverage Suboptimal, On-Policy Data**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2404.14367) — the abstract: methods that sample on-policy or push down the likelihood of some responses outperform offline and maximum-likelihood objectives
- Rafailov et al., **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2406.02900) — the abstract: DPO-style methods have no reward model yet degrade in a similar way at larger KL budgets, often within a single epoch

**RLVR and GRPO**
- Shao et al., **DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models**, arXiv:2402.03300 (2024) — **the original source of GRPO: §4.1, a section, not a paper of its own**; §5.2.1 writes SFT, DPO, PPO and GRPO as one gradient (Table 10); **preprint**
- DeepSeek-AI, **DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning**, *Nature* 645, 633–638 (2025; arXiv:2501.12948) — the abstract: reasoning behaviour elicited by pure RL, without human-labelled reasoning trajectories
- Lambert et al., **Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2411.15124) — **where the name RLVR comes from**, and a fully open recipe; the paper uses length-normalised DPO for the preference stage, with preference data generated by models and judged by an LLM, and PPO for the RLVR stage
- Yu et al., **DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2503.14476) — four techniques: clip-higher, dynamic sampling, a token-level loss, overlong reward shaping
- Liu et al., **Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2503.20783) — Dr. GRPO; the abstract: GRPO has an optimisation bias that artificially lengthens responses, wrong ones especially
- Zheng et al., **Group Sequence Policy Optimization**, arXiv:2507.18071 (2025) — GSPO; the abstract: the importance ratio is defined on the whole sequence and clipped at sequence level; it stabilises RL training of MoE models; **preprint**
- Gao et al., **Soft Adaptive Policy Optimization**, arXiv:2511.20347 (2025) — SAPO; the abstract: a smooth, temperature-controlled gate replaces hard clipping; **preprint**
- Bay & Yearick, **GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO Are Three Operations on One Number: The Group-Standard-Deviation Identity**, arXiv:2607.00152 (2026) — the identity for binary rewards (Theorem 1); **a two-author preprint**: the theorem leaves out clipping and the KL term, and the experiments use a toy policy. The three lines of algebra done in class are this identity
- Zhou et al., **Demystifying Group Relative Policy Optimization: Its Policy Gradient is a U-Statistic**, arXiv:2603.01162 (2026), and Wu et al., **It Takes Two: Your GRPO Is Secretly DPO**, arXiv:2510.00977 (2025; a NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper) — two theoretical readings of GRPO: the statistics of using the group mean as a baseline, and its relation to a contrastive objective; **neither is a main-conference paper**
- Cui et al., **The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models**, arXiv:2505.22617 (2025) — the abstract: policy entropy drops sharply early in training and performance saturates with it; Clip-Cov and KL-Cov; **preprint**
- Lightman et al., **Let's Verify Step by Step**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2305.20050); Wang et al., **Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations**, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2312.08935); Zhang et al., **The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning**, Findings of ACL 2025 (arXiv:2501.07301) — three papers on outcome versus process supervision; W10 picks them up

**Fooling the examiner: reward hacking, and what a reward actually measures**
- Skalse et al., **Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking**, arXiv:2209.13085 (2022) — the definition
- Shao et al., **Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2506.10947, v2 February 2026) — **assigned reading this week (in full)**; the abstract: random rewards raise Qwen2.5-Math-7B's MATH-500 score by 21.4 points against 29.1 for ground-truth rewards; the explanation offered is a bias from the clip term that amplifies behaviours with a high prior; other model families show no such gain
- Wu et al., **Reasoning or Memorization? Unreliable Results of Reinforcement Learning Due to Data Contamination**, AAAI 2026 (arXiv:2507.10532) — **assigned reading this week (§4.1 and §4.3)**; the abstract: Qwen2.5 shows data contamination on the commonly used benchmarks; on freshly generated arithmetic problems only correct rewards give steady improvement
- Yu et al., **Outcome Rewards Do Not Guarantee Verifiable or Causally Important Reasoning**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2604.22074) — the abstract: RLVR raises accuracy but does not reliably raise the causal importance or the sufficiency of the reasoning; a little SFT beforehand, or auxiliary rewards, can remedy this
- Helff et al., **LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking**, arXiv:2604.15149 (2026; a workshop paper) — the abstract: a verifier that checks only extensional correctness leads models to enumerate labels instead of inducing a rule; the behaviour appears in RLVR-trained reasoning models
- Khalifa et al., **Countdown-Code: A Testbed for Studying The Emergence and Generalization of Reward Hacking in RLVR**, EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2603.07084) — the abstract: 1% of reward-hacking trajectories in the SFT data is enough for a model to internalise the behaviour, which RL then amplifies and generalises
- Zhong, Raghunathan & Carlini, **ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2510.20270)
- Moya, Thornley & Lin, **Verifier Errors in RLVR: Reward Hacking, Limits of Feedback, and Selective Control**, arXiv:2609.35677 (2026) — the abstract: with an imperfect verifier held fixed, the conditions under which reward rises while correctness falls; **preprint**
- Wang et al., **Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: Mechanisms, Emergent Misalignment, Challenges**, arXiv:2604.13602 (2026) — a survey; **preprint**
- Kalai et al., **Why Language Models Hallucinate**, arXiv:2509.04664 (2025) — the abstract: training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty; **preprint**

**What RL costs, and what it changes**
- Khatri et al., **The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs**, ICLR 2026, oral (arXiv:2510.13786) — ScaleRL; the abstract: more than 400,000 GPU-hours; compute–performance curves are sigmoidal; loss aggregation, normalisation, curriculum and the off-policy algorithm mainly affect efficiency and barely move the asymptote
- Cheng et al., **IsoCompute Playbook: Optimally Scaling Sampling Compute for LLM RL**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2603.12151) — the abstract: the compute-optimal number of rollouts per problem rises with the budget and then saturates; the number of problems per batch mainly affects stability
- Mukherjee et al., **Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.11711) — the abstract: RL updates only 5%–30% of the parameters, and training that subnetwork alone recovers the performance
- Zhu et al., **ISO: An RLVR-Native Optimization Stack**, arXiv:2607.19331 (2026, v2 October 2026) — the abstract: RLVR reuses the base model's weight spectra and adapts the singular frames; the same kind of measurement as last week's intruder dimensions; **preprint**
- Shenfeld, Pari & Agrawal, **RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2509.04259); Chen et al., **Retaining by Doing: The Role of On-Policy Data in Mitigating Forgetting**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2510.18874); Chu et al., **SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training**, ICML 2025 (arXiv:2501.17161) — the three papers carried over from last week
- Schulman & Thinking Machines Lab, **LoRA Without Regret**, Thinking Machines Lab **blog**, 2025-09-29 — last week's blog post; the claim used this week is that under RL a rank-1 LoRA matches full fine-tuning. **Not peer-reviewed**

**On-policy distillation (shared with W11)**
- Agarwal et al., **On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.13649) — GKD; **one of the academic sources of the method**; the abstract: the student is trained on sequences it generated itself, with feedback from the teacher
- Gu et al., **MiniLLM: On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.08543) — the abstract: reverse KL replaces forward KL, with an on-policy method to optimise it
- Yang et al., **Qwen3 Technical Report**, arXiv:2505.09388 (2025) — the method used for shipped small models; **a technical report**
- Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, **On-Policy Distillation**, Thinking Machines Lab **blog**, 2025-10-27 (DOI 10.64434/tml.20251026) — **the widely circulated account; a blog post, not peer-reviewed**. It cites the three sources above itself. The 2×2 of sampling against signal density, and the remark that RL teaches a fixed number of bits per episode, come from here
- Song & Zheng, **A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2604.00626 (2026), and Li et al., **Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models: Phenomenology, Mechanism, and Recipe**, arXiv:2604.13016 (2026; a workshop paper) — two 2026 overviews; **preprints**

**Survey, and the way into next week**
- Zhang et al., **A Survey of Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models**, arXiv:2509.08827 (2025, 120 pages) — the most complete survey of this area so far; **preprint**
- Yue et al., **Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?**, NeurIPS 2025, oral (arXiv:2504.13837) — next week's reading; the abstract: at large $k$ the base model overtakes the RLVR-trained model in pass@$k$

**Tools**
- The source of Hugging Face `trl` v1.13.0, `trl/trainer/grpo_config.py` (the three arguments `loss_type`, `scale_rewards`, `importance_sampling_level` and their documentation) — **source code, not literature**; used this week as supporting evidence that the variants are switches
